The author uses these two items which people usually, rightly, associate with weight gain as examples of how cravings can be established via what they call the 'reward circuit'. There is an overwhelming experimental basis for this pathway which is distinguished from what they call 'metabolic hunger'. 'Fats' and 'sugar' are far more similar than some of the other things they present as examples of this circuit ie 'cocaine' and 'gambling'. The cravings for these things, and many other things called rightly or wrongly 'addictions', operate via the same mechanism.

As to your own particular case I'd hesitate to comment as I am not a nutritionist. What I can say is the following. Decades ago I first read literature claiming that 95% of diets on the market fall into three categories ie 1)Are harmful, 2)Don't work or 3)Result in a temporary weight loss that soon rebounds. Little has changed over the years. Let's ignore item #1 as you are still alive. Item #3 can only be seen from the future. Look at item #2. When a scientific paper concludes that something doesn't work all that it means is that the overall results are not statistically significant. All the data will present as standard curves with some outliers. If you are amongst that population that is more than 1 standard deviation away from the mean consider yourself lucky, but your experience can't be generalized or recommended. One might also ask what sort of exercise program you adopted or ask if you are a person with particularly strong will power.

As another anecdote I'd present the following. Once upon a surgery the last words the surgeon said to me as I left his office was "lose some weight". So I did. 2 to 3 months of no red meat, only fish and only small amounts of that. Practically no carbohydrates. Religious adherence to an exercise program. At the end I had lost 15 to 20 pounds. At the lower end of the estimate this would be equivalent to 120 pounds in two years. That being said I'd hesitate to recommend what I did as anything more than a general statement.

And you based that diet on what, exactly? I based mine on the scientific principles of ketogenic adaptation: it didn't only consist of "don't eat that" and it's practiced by a lot of people, not just me. Just FYI, I have no will power when it comes to food, my weight loss happened 4 years ago and only lasted 1.5 years but I never regained any weight, even when I resumed eating a "balanced" diet; I actually lost a few more pounds just by saying no to sweet food (it's easier when you get used to not eating sweet because the taste becomes unbearable).

I'm not recommending this diet to anyone, though, especially to someone whose condition doesn't depend on insulin resistance. I'm just saying that if I switched my 60% fat - 39% protein - 1% carb macronutrient ratios to 60% sugar etc. instead, I would ended up in a hospital. Not exactly a scientific approach to the matter, but it's enough to say fat and sugar might be chemically similar but are not equivalent at all. In general, I couldn't take such a simplistic concept seriously even if I never had such an experience.

Hello,

I tried to generate a discussion on this with my local (geographic) Reddit community, to the sound of crickets. I still think I should give it more time there, but I have my fingers crossed that this place would be more receptive. I am not interested in just theory, I want to help MAKE, and I want to do it as soon as possible.

To cut the chase, my opinion is that Bitcoin is a far from finished project. Novel life alterations that we may take for granted in 10 years,might not have been thought of yet but they're already possible with Bitcoin. Some have been thought of, but rarely used locally. This one has surely been thought of, but if it has I haven't heard of it.

The idea is this: Any sharing app takes a fee to itself. Whether it's the app that lets you rent/lend homes, the app that lets you rent/lend your car, the app that lets you hire a driver/sell your driving time.. or anything else. They all rely on people sharing things they already own with other people... and the marketplace takes a cut. For every transaction, they profit. And they should, they control the marketplace, provide service, etc...

But with Bitcoin, there could theoretically exist a decentralized local marketplace for all those things, without the middleman fees. An actual situation, where no service has 'liability' over what their users do, the service is run peer-to-peer; autonomously through the Bitcoin protocol and blockchain software (here is where I'm a little bit less of an expert than I'd like to be.) Going further than sharing apps, we share our opinions more than anything. Our voices, thoughts shouldn't be subject to some private TOS if we don't want it to be. Any microblogging/social media app comes with their own terms, for using their site. Why can't we have an unowned, decentralized service, funded by some automatically deducting fee to cover its networking costs?

After some research I discovered an open source project called Twister that aims to be a decentralized microblogging tool, which is great! But I don't think there is anywhere near enough the attention being spent on these matters as there should be.

I've had these thoughts for a while but the importance of them was just magnified. Seeing Ian's twitter just taken down sent chills down my spine. This is what he used to try to get his last words out. We need to have better.

I'm looking forward to hearing all opinions, and especially so from people who are already on this page.
